readerTitle: Nine reasons, no decision: how to group an argument so it lands
caseNote: 가상 사례 (매장 일요일 영업 제안, 전기 시공업체 장비·인력 제안) · 개념은 Minto의 피라미드 원칙에 바탕
insight: 설득력은 이유의 개수가 아니라 묶음에서 나온다. 서로 겹치지 않는 두세 개의 기둥으로 묶으면 듣는 사람은 결론을 기억하고, 반대할 때도 기둥 하나만 따져 볼 수 있다.
misconception: 이유를 많이 댈수록 주장이 강해진다. 좋은 이유를 전부 나열하면 상대가 알아서 납득한다.

sources.text: Minto, B. The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking (주장 아래 근거를 묶어 쌓는 구조)

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 인물은 가상입니다. 실제 수치나 연구 결과는 인용하지 않았습니다.
Minto 책의 초판 연도와 판본은 게시 전 확인이 필요합니다. 카드 본문에는 책 이름이나 연도를 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Nine good reasons. No decision.
body: Dana manages a home goods store. She wants to open on Sundays, so she emails the owner nine reasons why.
Every reason is true. The owner replies two days later: "Interesting. Let's talk about it sometime."
Nothing was wrong with her reasons. Something was wrong with how they were arranged.

image.label: An email with a long list of nine bullet points
image.brief: 매장 카운터 위 노트북 화면에 아홉 줄짜리 긴 글머리표 이메일. 화면 옆에 답장 말풍선 "Let's talk sometime". 따뜻한 매장 조명, 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Dana rewrite it?
body: Her nine reasons include: the mall next door is busy on Sundays, two rivals already open, customers keep asking, part-timers want more hours, weekend shoppers buy bigger items, and a few more.
She gets one more try. What should she do?

options.text: Keep all nine, but put the strongest first
options.feedback: Better order helps, but the owner still has to sort nine mixed points in his head. Most of them will blur together.

options.text: Sort them into three groups, each answering a different question the owner will have
options.feedback: The owner gets three ideas to weigh instead of nine to remember. You trade some detail up front for a message he can actually hold.

options.text: Cut to the single strongest reason
options.feedback: Short and clear, but one reason is easy to knock down. If he doubts it, the whole case falls with it.

cards.title: She made the reader do the sorting.
body: Look closely and Dana's nine reasons are really three kinds of reason mixed together.
Some say Sundays will bring sales. Some say the store can handle it. Some say the risk is low. A few even repeat each other: "the mall is busy" and "customers keep asking" both point to demand.
Scattered across a list, they read like nine small points. The owner had to find the pattern himself, and he didn't have time.

cards.title: Structure your argument
body: To **structure an argument**, put one claim on top. Under it, place two to four groups of reasons. Under each group, place the facts that back it.
Each group should answer a different question the listener will ask. Together they should cover the doubts that matter most.
The details are still there. They just sit underneath, where the listener can dig in only if they want to.

image.label: A pyramid: one claim on top, three supports, facts below
image.brief: 단순한 피라미드 다이어그램. 맨 위 상자 "Open on Sundays", 그 아래 세 상자 "It brings sales", "We can run it", "The risk is small", 각 상자 아래에 작은 점 두세 개. 플랫 일러스트, 차분한 색.

cards.title: Same facts, three supports.
body: Dana's second email fit on one screen. The owner replied the same day with one question about staffing.

breakdown.label: Open Sundays, starting next month
breakdown.detail: The one thing she wants decided

breakdown.label: It brings sales
breakdown.detail: Busy mall next door, customers asking, bigger weekend baskets

breakdown.label: We can run it
breakdown.detail: Part-timers want hours, no new hires needed

breakdown.label: The risk is small
breakdown.detail: An eight-week trial we can end anytime

cards.title: Now the owner can push back on one piece.
body: When the owner asked about staffing, the debate shrank to one support. Dana could answer it without defending the whole idea again.
That is a quiet benefit of structure. A listener who doubts one part can say so, and you know exactly where to bring more proof. With a flat list, one doubt tends to sink everything.
cards.softwareNote: A product lead pitching a new feature might group reasons as *users need it*, *we can build it*, and *it pays back*. When engineering questions the build estimate, the discussion stays on that one support instead of reopening the whole roadmap.

cards.title: A neat shape can hide a weak support.
body: Structure makes thin reasons look solid. If one group rests on a guess, say so plainly. Hiding it inside a tidy box only delays the hard question.
Don't force a magic number either. Two strong groups beat three where one is padding.
And check for overlap. If two groups are really the same reason twice, the argument looks wider than it is.

cards.title: Now it's an electrical contractor.
body: You co-own a small electrical firm. You want your partner to agree to a second van and an apprentice. How should you organize your case?

options.text: Tell the story of last year, month by month, and how busy it got
options.feedback: A story feels vivid, but your partner has to pull the reasons out of it. The key point may land in month nine, after attention has faded.

options.text: Group by question: there's enough work, it pays for itself, and we can scale back if work slows
options.feedback: Each group answers a worry your partner already has. If they doubt the payback, you know exactly which numbers to bring next.

options.text: Group by source: what I've seen, what customers say, what the crew says
options.feedback: It's organized, but by who said it, not by what it proves. Demand shows up in all three groups, and the cost question appears in none.

cards.title: Fewer, clearer supports beat a longer list.
body: Put one claim on top, then two to four groups that each answer a different doubt. The details go underneath.
**Try it today:** take a proposal you're about to send. Sort every reason under a heading, merge any that overlap, and check that each heading answers a question your reader will actually ask.
